newsitem.title: USA: James River, Fort Howard set $5.8 billion merger.
newsitem.headline: James River, Fort Howard set $5.8 billion merger.

text.p: James River Corp. and Fort Howard Corp. announced Monday a $5.8 billion merger that will create one of the world's largest makers of tissues, napkins and other paper products.
The new company will have annual sales of about $7 billion with brands such as Quilted Northern bathroom tissue, Brawny paper towels, Vanity Fair napkins and Dixie paper cups.

The union of the two companies into a new one called Fort James Corp. will create a diversified powerhouse with less exposure to the cyclical paper sector and more muscle to battle consumer companies like Kimberly-Clark Corp., industry experts said.
The companies called the formation of the new Fort James Corp. a merger of equals, but most of Wall Street viewed it as James River's acquisition of Fort Howard.
The companies said they expect few layoffs at the manufacturing level, although some overlap is expected in administrative areas. They were not specific.

"The broad North American focus of both companies, as well as their strong pan-European presence, represents a gateway to tremendous global opportunities," James River Chairman Miles Marsh said in a statement.

Under the deal, Fort Howard shareholders would get 1.375 shares of Fort James stock for each Fort Howard share, equal to $42.45 a share based on Friday's closing prices. Including assumption of Fort Howard debt, left from the company's buyout in the 1980s, the deal would be worth $5.8 billion.

Marsh will serve as Fort James's chairman and chief executive, and Michael Riordan, currently Fort Howard's chairman, will be president and chief operating officer. The 15-member board of the new company will be comprised of 11 directors from James River and four from Fort Howard.
James River and Fort Howard expect cost savings of $150 million in 1998 and more in later years from the merger from cutting jobs where there is duplication and improving efficiency.

At a news conference in New York to discuss the merger, executives said the new company will use Fort Howard's technology to develop new brands and expand into new markets. Industry experts said Fort Howard's key strength lies in the recycled paper business.

"Our new entity truly pushes forward the grand opportunities that lie ahead of us for worldwide growth. These two companies are ready to emerge as a powerful single force and industry leader in paper-based consumer groups," Marsh said at the press conference.

The new company will take a restructuring charge when the deal is completed, though the amount has not been set. Excluding the restructuring charge and other charges, the deal would add to earnings, the companies said.
Industry experts said the union will combine James River's strong consumer market position with Fort Howard's commercial presence and state-of-the-art facilities.
"I think it's something that James River had to do. It gives them a much stronger base to compete," said an investment banker who did not want to be identified.

Although already second to Kimberly-Clark, which strengthened its hand in 1995 by acquiring former rival Scott Paper Co. for $9.4 billion, the new company will now be much closer in size to Kimberly-Clark.
James River rose $1.75 to $32.625 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange while Fort Howard surged $6 to $42.50 in active trading on Nasdaq.

James River, based in Richmond, Va., had net earnings of $157.3 million, or $1.15 a share, on sales of about $5.7 billion in 1996. Fort Howard, based in Green Bay, Wis., earned $162.6 million, or $2.32 a share, on sales about $1.6 billion.
The deal has been approved by the boards of directors of both companies. It requires approval from regulators in the United States and Europe and from shareholders of both companies.
The transaction is likely to be closely scrutinised by the U.S. Department of Justice, which required divestitures before it approved the Kimberly-Clark union with Scott Paper.
Officials of both companies said they hoped the deal could be concluded without any asset sales. They also said they hoped the deal will be completed by the end of the summer.
The deal is meant to be tax-free to shareholders.
